overview.headline: How radioactivity and half-life build the numeric geologic time scale

keyPoints.point: Geologists use radioactivity to show Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
keyPoints.quote: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old?

keyPoints.point: Half-life is the length of time required for one-half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.
keyPoints.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

keyPoints.point: Isotopes of an element differ only in the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
keyPoints.quote: Isotopes of an element are atoms that differ from one another only in the number of neutrons in the nucleus.

keyPoints.point: Isotopic techniques measure the time at which a particular mineral within a rock was formed.
keyPoints.quote: Isotopic techniques are used to measure the time at which a particular mineral within a rock was formed.

keyTerms.gloss: Length of time required for one-half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms
keyTerms.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

keyTerms.gloss: Radioactive form that has its own unique half-life
keyTerms.quote: Each radioactive isotope has its own unique half-life.

keyTerms.gloss: Radioactive atom that decays to daughter at constant rate
keyTerms.quote: The change from parent to daughter happens at a constant rate, called the half-life.

keyTerms.gloss: Product of many years of detective work using dating techniques to order rock and fossil history
keyTerms.quote: The geologic time scale is the product of many years of detective work, as well as a variety of dating techniques not discussed here.
